_meta.description: Limb E in operational form. The fiscal arithmetic, the scheduled policy events, the step functions markets price late, and the reimbursement exposure map that constrains how the limb D book is built.
_meta.verify_note: Sourced against the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released 9 June 2026) on 2026-08-07. These figures move with every annual report — the next edition resets them. The v1 estimate of 'mid-2030s' OASI depletion was wrong by roughly three years in the direction that matters.

headline.title: The thesis's own hedge
headline.body: The same demographics that guarantee healthcare volume make healthcare price the most politically exposed line in the federal budget. That is why limb E sits in the same dashboard as limb D rather than in a risk appendix — it is not an external shock to the thesis, it is a consequence of the thesis succeeding. Every position in the care book should be constructed so that an adverse reimbursement decision is survivable.

arithmetic.body: Fewer contributing workers per beneficiary each year, mechanically, as the cohort claims and the trailing edge stops contributing. This is the cleanest arithmetic in the thesis and the least contestable — it is the same population table the cohort clock is built from, read from the fiscal side. Census has 65+ going from 57.8M (2022) to 71.2M (2030) to 82.2M (2050), while the 55–64 band that feeds it contracts until 2035.

arithmetic.state: 2032 — three years sooner than v1 assumed
arithmetic.body: The forcing function, and the largest single correction to the v1 thesis. The 2026 Trustees Report puts OASI reserve depletion in 2032 (fourth quarter), with the combined OASDI funds at 2034 — not the mid-2030s quoted from memory. Depletion does not mean benefits stop: it means benefits become payable only from incoming receipts, which is 78% of scheduled benefits, declining toward 62% by 2100. That is a date-certain political event now sitting inside the horizon of most positions in this book rather than beyond it, and it is exactly the kind of step function markets price late and abruptly.

arithmetic.src: 2026 Trustees Report / Center for Retirement Research
arithmetic.body: A 16% deterioration in a single year, driven by three revisions: the fertility assumption cut from 1.90 to 1.75 children per woman, lower assumed immigration, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently reducing income tax revenue on Social Security benefits. In dollar terms the shortfall moved from roughly $26.1T to $30.3T. Two of those three revisions are demographic assumptions moving in the direction this thesis argues.

Mandatory spending growth against a shrinking relative contribution base means more borrowing, weighted long. This is where limb E collides with limb A: heavier long-end supply against a decumulating cohort's structural demand for duration. The term premium is where that argument gets settled, which is why it is on the indicator list as an arbiter rather than a position.

Enrolment is the cohort clock. Cost trend per beneficiary is partly limb C — care wages are the dominant input. The two compound, which is why healthcare is the line item under the most sustained pressure and why reimbursement risk is structural rather than cyclical.

arithmetic.state: The first place the squeeze lands
arithmetic.body: Long-term care is largely Medicaid-funded and Medicaid is a state budget line without a federal printing press behind it. State fiscal stress arrives as rate pressure on skilled nursing and personal care operators years before any federal entitlement legislation. This is the most underrated near-term policy risk in the universe.

step_functions.body: Resets the depletion date and the political clock with it. The single scheduled event that most moves limb E. Diary it rather than watching for it.

Sets the following year's benchmark rates and risk-model parameters. The tradable event for the payor vertical — the final Rate Announcement usually confirms the Advance Notice rather than departing from it.
Grinds down per-service reimbursement for outpatient providers, therapy and imaging year after year. Slow, cumulative, and the structural headwind under several otherwise attractive volume stories.
Directly sets the revenue line for skilled nursing and home health operators. Combined with state Medicaid rates, this is the entire margin question for the care vertical.

Benefit formula changes, means-testing, retirement age adjustment, payroll tax cap changes. Unforecastable in timing, transformative in effect, and the stated falsifier for limb E. A credible reform package repaths the fiscal limb and changes the reimbursement risk premium embedded across the whole care book.

Sits in this file because it is policy, but it is the largest swing factor in the entire thesis rather than a fiscal item. A sustained surge relieves the constrained occupations, neutralises limb C and simultaneously repairs limb D's and limb H's cost problem — flipping several limbs at once.

reimbursement_map.title: Reimbursement exposure — the constraint on position construction
reimbursement_map.intro: Sorted by how much of the earnings stream depends on a rate set by government. This map is why the limb D book tilts toward private-pay and volume rather than toward the largest addressable market.

tiers.names: UNH, HUM, ALHC, ELV, CVS, ENSG, ADUS, AVAH, NHC, CHE, EHC, OHI, CTRE, SBRA
tiers.note: Earnings depend on a CMS benchmark or a state Medicaid rate. Own only where operating competence is genuinely differentiated, and cap the aggregate share of the book.

tiers.names: SYK, ZBH, BSX, EW, MDT, GMED, USPH, RDNT, LH, OPCH, WELL, VTR, BKD
tiers.note: Procedure or facility revenue is reimbursed, but volume growth and mix can outrun rate erosion. The thesis needs volume to win that race — track it as an operating metric, not an assumption.

tiers.names: ALC (premium IOL), SOON.SW, DEMANT.CO, AMP.MI, COH.AX, STMN.SW, SCI, CSV, MATW, MCK, COR, CAH, KMB, ESSITY-B.ST, 8113.T
tiers.note: Private-pay, or volume-and-mix distribution with no drug-price exposure. This tier is the deliberate structural hedge against limb E and the reason the private-pay theme scores as highly as it does.

political_economy.title: Why the price risk and not the volume risk
political_economy.body: The cohort is the most reliable voting bloc in the country, which makes benefit cuts to beneficiaries politically expensive and payments to providers politically cheap. The historical pattern is consistent: when the fiscal squeeze arrives, it lands on provider reimbursement and on the payors administering the programmes long before it lands on the benefit itself. That asymmetry is the single most useful thing to know when constructing the limb D book — it says the volume is safe and the price is not, and it points the whole portfolio toward businesses paid by patients rather than by programmes.
